In Matthew chapter 28, we see a living pattern of worship revealed at the resurrection. The women — including Mary Magdalene — bowed before Yeshua. They did not worship Him as the only true God in abstraction, but they honored Him as the Son of God, obeyed the revelation given, and responded faithfully. This is relational worship: bow, work, serve, obey.

Christ did not assert independent deity; He was given power over all heaven and earth by the Father, and He gave part of that authority to the disciples to carry the Kingdom mission. This is worship in obedience and delegated service — not mere sentiment.

Pilate’s wife had a dream warning her not to harm the just man, showing that truth confronts even the worldly mind. The mob chose Barabbas, not Yeshua — a riotous choice that reflects the kind of companionship Proverbs condemns. When Pilate washed his hands, claiming innocence, the crowd declared, “His blood be on us and on our children.” This is a self‑chosen covenant of rejection at the cost of truth.

At the cross, mockers say, “If You are the Son of God…” — not God in the flesh. Even in scorn, they affirm His identity as Son. Watch Gospel Lesson

Proverbs 19:15 (KJV)

“Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger.”

This verse speaks to the condition of the psyche (soul) — the internal life of imagination, intention, and attention. A soul that is idle — without creative motion, purpose, or disciplined activation — descends into a “deep sleep” of unawareness, passivity, and lack. This is not merely physical rest, but a disengagement of the psyche from meaningful obedience and Kingdom participation. An idle psyche suffers hunger because it fails to activate imagination, intention, and skill toward God’s way.
